summary:
Gwangju stands under South Korea's national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive. In 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented trans-specific harm is the case of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical prerequisite has fallen away. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is against the law and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria; the court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is the most concrete on-the-ground protection for a visitor. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award on a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change a court had approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The first-instance judgment had issued on 2 July 2024 from the Seoul Central District Court with no appeal on that point. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear.

Facility avoidance extends to schools. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose; a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
The trans-specific rulings a visitor relies on were handed down in Seoul and in Yeongdong, not in Gwangju, and they bind nationwide rather than locally. Gwangju is therefore scored on the national framework, with no city-level ordinance on gender identity or sex-segregated facilities located in this source set.

Hostility at public gatherings is concentrated elsewhere on the calendar: the Incheon Pride attack and the 2,000-officer Busan deployment in 2018 show the scale of protest mobilisation that Pride organisers have had to absorb, which shapes what a visitor can expect at any Pride event in the country.

The 2025 nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults and the 2014, 2018 and 2021 survey findings describe a discrimination burden that sits behind the legal advances, since no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute converts those findings into an enforceable claim.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records a comparatively positive environment for free media and civil society, which means hostile conduct is documented and litigated rather than concealed, but it does not remove the underlying risk to individuals.

The 24 November 2022 Supreme Court en banc ruling allows transgender people with minor children to obtain recognition provided they are not married.

Residents who have completed a family-register gender change are covered by the final 22 July 2024 appellate judgment, which treats comfortable restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right and holds police advice to avoid women's public restrooms an infringement of personal rights.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Gwangju-specific source appears in this inventory; every finding above is drawn from national or other-city material and is presented as the framework Gwangju is scored against. Whether Gwangju operates any local anti-discrimination ordinance, city human-rights charter provision on gender identity, or municipal guideline for public facilities is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether Military Criminal Act article 92-6 has been enforced against personnel stationed in or attached to units in Gwangju is not sourced.

The destination and outcome of the government's appeal in the 2017 NGO registration litigation, noted as continuing, is unresolved in this inventory.

It is unresolved whether the Ministry of Health and Welfare has since issued the hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients that the National Human Rights Commission of Korea requested in November 2023.

The current posture of charges filed by Pride organisers against pastors in Incheon, and of their allegation of police inaction, is not sourced beyond the filing.
